question: What is the main job of sensory receptors in your nervous system?

options.A: To send final motor commands to skeletal muscles
options.B: To produce hormones that regulate body temperature
options.C: To monitor changes inside and outside the body
options.D: To integrate information inside the spinal cord

explanation: You've got this! Sensory receptors are like your body's watchmen—they catch what's happening around and inside you and report it back to the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h1)

question: When your brain interprets information and decides what to do about it, what is this process called?
explanation: Think of integration as your brain's processing unit making sense of all the clues it receives. Great job keeping up with your nursing studies! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which two main organs make up the Central Nervous System (CNS)?
explanation: Always remember, the CNS is just the heavy-duty command center: the brain and the spinal cord. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)?

options.A: To act as communication lines linking the body to the CNS
options.B: To process and integrate complex memories
options.C: To produce cerebrospinal fluid for the brain
options.D: To directly control hormonal release in the pituitary gland

explanation: The PNS acts like telephone wires, carrying messages back and forth between your body and the central control unit. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which part of the brain is your go-to area for balance and coordination?
explanation: The cerebellum keeps you steady on your feet and helps coordinate your movements so you don't trip over your scrubs! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h3)

question: What protective layers wrap around both the brain and the spinal cord?
explanation: The meninges are like sturdy cushion layers wrapped around your delicate central nervous system for safety. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which pathway carries nerve signals toward the central nervous system?
explanation: A-fferent arrives at the brain (think 'A' for arrival). You'll master these terms in no time! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h4)

question: You touch a hot pot in the clinical kitchen and instantly pull your hand back. Which fibers carried the signal from your CNS out to your hand muscles?
explanation: E-fferent exits the brain with instructions (think 'E' for exit). Quick reflexes keep future nurses safe! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which part of the nervous system lets you consciously control your skeletal muscles to walk or write?
explanation: The somatic system handles voluntary movements—the things you decide to do on purpose. Keep pushing forward! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h5)

question: Your heart beats and your food digests automatically without you having to think about it. Which system runs this show?
explanation: The autonomic system runs automatically in the background so you can focus on your nursing notes. Well done! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which body reaction is a classic sign of the sympathetic nervous system kicking in?
explanation: Think 'fight or flight'! When stress or excitement hits, your heart races to pump more blood. You've got this concept down. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h6)

question: When a patient is resting peacefully after a good meal, which part of their nervous system is hard at work?
explanation: Think 'rest and digest'! The parasympathetic system takes over when it's time to chill and recover energy. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is the main job of neurons?

options.A: To form the bony skull protection
options.C: To provide structural division without signaling

explanation: Neurons are the electrical wiring specialists of the body, sending messages back and forth like tiny messengers. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h7)

question: How do neuroglial cells differ from neurons?

options.A: Neurons provide physical support rather than signaling.
options.B: Glial cells are incapable of cell division.
options.C: Neurons are much smaller than neuroglial cells.
options.D: Glial cells do not transmit nerve impulses.

explanation: Glial cells are the supportive helpers and cheerleaders for neurons, but they don't carry the electrical signals themselves. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h7)

question: A patient reports numbness in just one hand after a minor wrist injury. Which part of the nervous system is most likely involved?
explanation: Localized issues in a limb usually point to a peripheral nerve problem in that exact area. Brilliant deduction! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h8)

question: Why does damage to the central nervous system usually affect the whole body more drastically than an injury to a single peripheral nerve?

options.A: The CNS serves as the primary integration and control center.
options.B: Neuroglial cells in the PNS cannot repair themselves.
options.C: The CNS does not have protective meninges.
options.D: Peripheral nerves lack any sensory fibers.

explanation: Because the CNS is the master control unit for everything, any trouble there has a much wider ripple effect across the body. You are crushing these questions! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h8)
